audience: Students learning a visual proof of a sequence identity
question: Show why the sum of the first n odd numbers equals n squared, not just a few numerical examples.

acts.beat: Represent the first odd number as a one-by-one square.
Show each next odd number forming a new L-shaped border.
Count each border and identify its general odd number.
Explain why n borders form an n-by-n square.

panels.title: Begin with one
panels.question: What does the first odd number build?
panels.new_idea: The number 1 is exactly the cell count of a one-by-one square.
panels.caption: One cell makes a one-by-one square.

panels.title: Add the next odd number
panels.question: What happens when three is added?
panels.new_idea: Three cells form an L-shaped border around the original square, making a two-by-two square.
panels.caption: Adding three completes the next square.

panels.title: The border pattern
panels.question: Why are the added amounts always odd?
panels.new_idea: Growing an (n−1)-by-(n−1) square to n-by-n adds n cells along one side and n−1 along the other: 2n−1.
panels.caption: Each new border contains n plus n−1 cells.

panels.title: The general result
panels.question: Why does the sum equal n squared?
panels.new_idea: Starting from one, successive odd-number borders assemble exactly an n-by-n square containing n² cells.
panels.caption: Every odd layer fills one larger square.

takeaway: The first n odd numbers are successive L-shaped borders of an n-by-n square, so their sum is n².
